title: Building a Culture for a Kubernetes-Based Platform in a Bank
gist: At KubeCon & CloudNativeCon Europe, Marcy Paramonova and Stéphane Cusin described how an (unnamed) bank's Kubernetes platform succeeded only after it built a culture of ownership, a community of practice and bottom-up experimentation, with open source winning trust by running real workloads. Their second-generation platform hides Kubernetes behind opinionated, standardized delivery patterns, and the team is now watching OpenStack the same way it once spotted Kubernetes.

themes.theme: Open source adoption in regulated banking

insights.claim: In the bank described by Paramonova and Cusin, open source was initially questioned over support and accountability, and trust was won not through argument but by running real production workloads on the platform day after day.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Regulated buyers adopt open-source infrastructure through operational proof, which favors vendors and projects with demonstrable production track records.
insights.quote: Open source stopped being seen as a risk. It became the foundation.
insights.locator: Open source was not an obvious choice

insights.claim: The bank's platform team uses open-source health signals (strong community, transparent governance, real production users) as a 'compass' for technology choices; it recognized Kubernetes this way and is now evaluating OpenStack using the same lens.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Enterprise interest in OpenStack as a next open-source bet signals possible demand for private-cloud alternatives inside banks.
insights.quote: The compass pointed; we followed. And now we are watching OpenStack the same way.
insights.locator: They used open source as a compass

themes.theme: Culture as the bottleneck for platform success

insights.claim: The bank's first Kubernetes platform was delivered as a project and achieved good adoption, but operations became extremely hard because responsibilities were blurry, teams consumed without contributing, and every incident felt like a fire drill.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Platform-engineering spend often fails on operating model rather than technology, creating demand for ownership/operations tooling and services.
insights.quote: Without that culture, no platform survives its own success.

insights.claim: Paramonova and Cusin argue that deploying Kubernetes is the easy part and the hard part is building a community of practice with shared knowledge, rituals and an ownership model, with structure designed first and culture following.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Cloud-native transformation timelines in large enterprises are gated by organizational change, slowing realized ROI.

insights.claim: The bank drives bottom-up improvement through a yearly competition in which anyone can submit ideas and the winning idea is actually implemented.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Minor color on how incumbent banks try to foster engineering innovation internally.

insights.claim: The bank's first platform version exposed many Kubernetes capabilities and allowed extensive customization, which led to divergent deployment patterns across teams; the current version instead offers opinionated deployment patterns and standardized Helm charts.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Supports the internal-developer-platform thesis: value accrues to abstraction layers that standardize delivery, not raw Kubernetes flexibility.
insights.quote: In our current platform, Kubernetes is no longer the product. Kubernetes is the implementation detail.

insights.claim: According to Cusin, developers come to a platform to deliver software rather than for more infrastructure choices, so standardization means engineers moving between teams do not need to relearn packaging, deployment, monitoring or operations.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Standardized golden paths reduce engineer onboarding cost, a key selling point for platform-engineering products.
insights.quote: developers do not come to a platform looking for more infrastructure choices. They come to a platform to deliver software.
insights.locator: One of the lessons we learned

insights.claim: Paramonova says Kubernetes' biggest impact was organizational: it gave teams a common language and shared abstractions that eased collaboration across previously siloed teams and technology stacks.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Kubernetes' entrenchment as an enterprise lingua franca reinforces ecosystem lock-in for tooling built on it.
